pages.summary: Show a value without its name.
body: Shows a value as the Command Window shows a variable, but without the `name =` line and the blank lines around it. Text is shown as it is, without quotes. To mix text and numbers on one line, build the text with `sprintf`, `num2str` or string concatenation, or use `fprintf`.

examples.title: Text and a number together
examples.output:
The answer is 42
Strings join with +: 42

pages.summary: Write formatted text to the Command Window or to a file.
body: The format is text with conversions that the values fill in turn: `%d` an integer, `%f` a fixed-point number (`%.2f` with two decimals), `%e` exponential notation, `%g` the shorter of the two, `%s` text, `%%` a percent sign; `\n` ends a line and `\t` is a tab. A width before the letter pads the field (`%8.3f`). When there are more values than conversions, the format is used again, which prints a table from a matrix (its columns in turn). With a file identifier from `fopen` first, the text goes to that file.
syntax: Writes the formatted values to the Command Window.
Writes to the file `fid` (1 is the Command Window).
With the number of bytes written.
inputs: The format, with conversions such as `%d`, `%.3f`, `%s` and `\n`.

examples.title: Numbers with a chosen number of decimals
examples.code:
fprintf('pi is about %.4f\n', pi)
fprintf('%d apples and %d pears\n', 3, 5)
examples.output:
pi is about 3.1416
3 apples and 5 pears

examples.title: A table from a matrix
examples.intro: The format is used for each pair of values, taken down the columns of the matrix.
examples.output:
1 squared is   1
 2 squared is   4
 3 squared is   9
 4 squared is  16

examples.title: Text, widths and exponential notation

body: Takes the same formats as `fprintf` but returns the text instead of showing it. The format is used again until every value is written: `sprintf('%d,', 1:3)` is `'1,2,3,'`.
syntax: The formatted text, as a character vector.

examples.title: A list joined by the format

pages.summary: A number as text, with about four significant decimals by default.
body: Turns numbers into a character vector for display: integers as they are, others with up to four decimals (about five significant digits). A precision gives that many significant digits, and a format string works as in `sprintf`. A matrix gives a row of text for each row.

examples.title: A message with a number in it

pages.summary: Text as a double; NaN when it is not a number.
body: Reads text such as `'3.14'`, `'-2e5'` or `'Inf'` as a number. Text that is not a number gives `NaN`, so the result can be checked with `isnan`. A cell array or string array of texts gives an array of numbers.
syntax: The number in the text `s` (or each text of a cell or string array).

examples.title: Numbers in text, and text that is not one
Checking user input

pages.summary: Join text; trailing spaces of char arrays are dropped.
body: Joins its arguments end to end. Trailing spaces of character arrays are removed first (those of strings and cells are kept), which is why `['abc ', 'def']` keeps the space and `strcat('abc ', 'def')` does not. With a cell array, each cell is joined to the others; with a string, the result is a string.

pages.summary: Split text at a separator (white space by default).
body: The pieces between the separators, as a cell row. Without a separator the text is split at white space; a cell array of separators splits at any of them. Separators next to each other count as one, unless `'CollapseDelimiters'` is false: then an empty piece lies between them.
syntax: Split at `delimiter` (a text, or a cell array of texts).
With an empty piece between separators next to each other.

examples.title: Words, and comma-separated values
examples.code:
words = strsplit('the quick brown fox')
parts = strsplit('a,b,,c', ',')
kept = strsplit('a,b,,c', ',', 'CollapseDelimiters', false)

examples.title: Several separators, and numbers from text

pages.summary: Join the text of a cell array with a separator (a space by default).
body: The opposite of `strsplit`: the cells' texts joined, with the separator between each pair.

examples.title: Spaces and commas
examples.output:
ans =

    'one two three'

ans =

    'one, two, three'

pages.summary: Replace every occurrence of a substring.
body: Finds `old` in the text and puts `new` in its place, every time it occurs. The match is exact and case-sensitive; for patterns use `regexprep`. Works on each element of a cell or string array.

examples.title: Replacing words and characters
examples.code:
strrep('the cat sat on the mat', 'at', 'og')
strrep('2024/03/15', '/', '-')
examples.output:
ans =

    'the cog sog on the mog'

ans =

    '2024-03-15'

examples.title: In each cell

pages.summary: Text in capitals or in small letters.
body: Changes the case of letters and leaves other characters as they are. Works on character arrays, cell arrays of text and string arrays. Case-insensitive comparisons often lower both sides first, or use `strcmpi`.

pages.summary: True when text contains a pattern.
body: Whether a pattern occurs anywhere in the text. For a cell or string array it answers for each element; a cell array of patterns asks whether any of them occurs. `'IgnoreCase'` makes it case-insensitive.

examples.title: Any of several patterns, and case
examples.code:
contains("Report FINAL", "final", 'IgnoreCase', true)
contains({'apple pie', 'banana', 'cherry tart'}, {'pie', 'tart'})

pages.summary: A string array, from text, numbers or cells.
body: A string holds a piece of text as one element, so an array of strings is an array of texts, each of its own length. Strings are written in double quotes, join with `+`, and compare with `==`. `string` makes them from character vectors, numbers (with up to about five significant digits) and cell arrays of text.

examples.title: From numbers and from a cell array
examples.output:
s =

  1×3 string array

    "1"    "2.5"    "1000000"

t =

  1×2 string array

    "red"    "green"
